title: MODULE 12 — Frontend Testing and Quality Engineering

overview.text: Building a frontend application is not enough. You must also prove that it works correctly, behaves consistently across browsers, handles unexpected situations and remains stable when developers introduce new changes.
Frontend Testing and Quality Engineering teaches you how professional engineering teams verify application quality before releasing software to users.
Consider a learning platform like PrepSpaces.
Every one of these interactions can contain defects.

For example, a student might successfully complete a lesson, but the progress indicator may not update. A login form might work in Chrome but fail in Safari. A mobile navigation menu might overlap the course content after a UI change.
Testing helps identify these problems before they reach users.
By the end of this module, you should be able to:
Understand why frontend testing is necessary.
Test React components using React Testing Library.
Test React hooks and custom hooks.
Verify forms, validations and user interactions.
Automate complete user journeys with Playwright.
Measure test coverage and software quality.
Testing foundations — Lessons 1–2: Understand testing principles, testing levels and the testing pyramid.
Unit and component testing — Lessons 3–7: Test JavaScript logic, React components, hooks, forms and external dependencies.
Application-level testing — Lessons 8–10: Test integrated features, browser journeys and cross-browser compatibility.
Quality assurance — Lessons 11–13: Verify accessibility, visual consistency and testing coverage.
Automated engineering workflows — Lesson 14: Integrate tests into CI pipelines and release processes.

blocks.text: 1.1 What is frontend testing?
Frontend testing is the process of verifying that a web application's interface, functionality, interactions and expected behavior work correctly.
You write test cases to verify whether the application produces the expected results under different conditions.
Consider a simple login form. A user enters an email address and password and clicks Login.
You should verify:
Whether valid credentials are accepted.
Whether incorrect credentials are rejected.
Whether an error message appears.
Whether empty fields are handled.
Whether the loading indicator works.
Whether the user is redirected after successful authentication.
Whether the form behaves correctly on mobile devices.
Testing ensures that these requirements are satisfied.
1.2 Why is frontend testing important?
Imagine you update a navigation component. The updated navigation works correctly on the homepage, but accidentally breaks the dashboard.
Without testing, you may discover the problem only after users report it.
1. Bug detection: Find errors before they reach production.
2. Regression prevention: Ensure that previously working functionality does not break after new changes.
3. Application reliability: Make sure important application features behave consistently.
4. Better code maintenance: Allow developers to modify existing components with greater confidence.
5. Improved user experience: Identify interaction problems, navigation errors and interface inconsistencies.
6. Faster development: Automated tests can repeatedly verify application behavior without requiring developers to manually check every feature after every change.
1.3 Understanding real-world frontend defects
Feature | Possible defect
Login | Valid users cannot log in
Registration | Duplicate account creation
Course catalogue | Incorrect courses displayed
Search | Search results do not update
Progress tracking | Completed lessons are not saved
Navigation | Broken links
Dashboard | Incorrect student information
Forms | Invalid input accepted
Mobile interface | Buttons overlap content
API integration | Loading screen never disappears
1.4 Manual testing vs automated testing

Manual testing: A human tester opens the application and performs actions. Useful for exploratory testing, usability problems, human judgement, and visual review, but repetitive, time-consuming, and difficult to repeat consistently.
Automated testing: Developers write code that automatically performs actions and verifies results.
This test can be executed repeatedly.
1.5 What is regression testing?

Regression testing verifies that modifications to an application have not broken existing functionality. It is particularly important in large applications because a change in one component can affect other parts of the system.
1.6 When should frontend testing happen?
Requirement -> Development -> Unit Testing -> Component Testing -> Integration Testing -> End-to-End Testing -> Quality Verification -> Production Release
Lesson outcome: Understand the importance of frontend testing, the difference between manual and automated testing, regression testing and how testing improves software reliability.

sections.title: Testing Strategies and the Testing Pyramid

blocks.text: 2.1 Understanding types of frontend tests
1. Unit testing: Tests a small independent piece of logic (e.g. course completion percentage calculation).
2. Component testing: Tests an individual React component (e.g. CourseCard title and button click).
3. Integration testing: Tests multiple components or services working together (e.g. search input + API service + results list).
4. End-to-End testing: Tests an entire user journey inside a real browser.
5. Visual regression testing: Checks whether a new application version has introduced unintended visual differences.
2.2 Understanding the testing pyramid
Testing pyramid (illustrative distribution, not a mandatory test-count ratio):
E2E tests — Few · Expensive
Integration tests — Moderate · Combined features
Unit and component tests — Many · Faster feedback
Bottom layer — Unit tests: Utility functions, data transformations, validation functions, calculations, reusable logic.
Middle layer — Integration tests: Form and validation, search and API, course card and navigation, auth state and dashboard.
Top layer — End-to-End tests: User registration, login and logout, course enrolment, lesson completion, search and filtering.
2.3 Understanding the AAA testing pattern
Arrange: Prepare the test environment and input.
Act: Perform the action being tested.
Assert: Verify the expected result.
2.4 Understanding test isolation

Every test should ideally be independent. Tests that depend on execution order are difficult to maintain and can produce inconsistent results. Playwright also recommends independently isolated tests so that state from one test does not affect another. (Playwright)
2.5 Choosing the correct testing level
Requirement | Best testing approach
Calculate progress percentage | Unit
Display course information | Component
Search and filter courses | Integration
Complete student enrolment | End-to-end
Detect broken mobile layout | Visual regression
Check keyboard navigation | Accessibility
Verify Chrome and Firefox behavior | Cross-browser
Lesson outcome: Understand the main types of testing, the testing pyramid, the AAA pattern, test isolation and how to choose the appropriate testing level.
3.1 What is unit testing?
Unit testing verifies that individual pieces of application logic (functions, TypeScript utilities, calculations, validations, transformations) produce the expected results.
3.2 What is Vitest?

Vitest is a testing framework designed for modern JavaScript and TypeScript projects. It provides test execution, assertions, grouping, mocking, spying, fake timers, code coverage, and watch mode. Vitest integrates naturally with Vite-based applications and can be used for suitable Next.js unit tests. (Vitest)
3.3 Installing Vitest

npm install -D vitest
npx vitest
Vitest discovers test files such as calculateProgress.test.ts or calculateProgress.spec.ts.
3.4 Writing your first unit test
src/utils/calculateProgress.ts
src/utils/calculateProgress.test.ts
3.5 Understanding important Vitest functions
Function | Responsibility
describe() | Groups related tests
it() | Defines a test case
test() | Alternative to it()
expect() | Checks expected results
beforeEach() | Runs before every test
afterEach() | Runs after every test
beforeAll() | Runs before a test group
afterAll() | Runs after a test group
vi.fn() | Creates a mock function
vi.spyOn() | Tracks or replaces an existing method
vi.mock() | Replaces module dependencies
3.6 Understanding assertions
toBe() checks identity or primitive equality; toEqual() checks deep equality of object structures.
3.7 Testing boundary conditions
Test zero completed lessons, zero total lessons, one completed lesson, all lessons completed, invalid negative values, and more completed lessons than total lessons.
3.8 Configuring Vitest for React projects
npm install -D vitest @vitejs/plugin-react jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/user-event @testing-library/jest-dom
vitest.config.ts
src/test/setup.ts
3.9 Understanding test scripts
Command | Purpose
npm run test | Runs tests in development watch mode (`vitest`)
npm run test:run | Runs tests once (`vitest run`)
npm run test:coverage | Runs tests and generates coverage reports (`vitest run --coverage`)
Lesson outcome: You should be able to install Vitest, create unit tests, use assertions, test boundary conditions and configure a React testing environment.

sections.title: Component Testing with React Testing Library

blocks.text: 4.1 What is component testing?
Component testing verifies the behavior of individual UI components (title, description, level, accessible controls, and click behavior).
4.2 What is React Testing Library?

React Testing Library tests React components through their rendered DOM. Its central philosophy is that tests should resemble how users interact with applications, testing visible output and user interactions rather than private component state. (Testing Library)
4.3 Understanding the render function
4.4 Understanding screen queries
Query | Purpose
getByRole() | Finds an element by accessible role
getByLabelText() | Finds an input using its label
getByText() | Finds visible text
getByPlaceholderText() | Finds an input using its placeholder
getByTestId() | Finds an element using a test ID
queryByText() | Useful when checking that something is absent
findByRole() | Waits asynchronously for an element
Prefer accessible queries such as getByRole() and getByLabelText() whenever possible. (Testing Library)
4.5 Building a testable React component
CourseCard.tsx
CourseCard.test.tsx
4.6 Testing conditional rendering
4.7 Testing component behavior instead of implementation details

Avoid checking private React state directly, internal function names, implementation-specific CSS classes, or internals users never interact with. Tests should continue passing when internals are refactored.
Lesson outcome: Understand React Testing Library, component rendering, accessible DOM queries, conditional rendering and user-oriented component testing.

sections.title: Testing React Hooks and Custom Hooks

blocks.text: 5.1 What is a custom hook?
5.2 Why test custom hooks?
A defect inside a shared custom hook (like course progress tracking) can affect every component that uses it.
5.3 Understanding renderHook
act() ensures React updates are applied before assertions are made. Testing behavior through an actual component is often preferable when that produces a clearer test. (Testing Library)
5.4 Testing initial values
5.5 Testing decrement behavior
5.6 Testing hooks with asynchronous behavior
Verify initial loading state, successful data retrieval, empty responses, API failures, retry behavior, and cleanup on unmount using waitFor() or findBy... queries.
5.7 Testing hooks with providers
When custom hooks depend on React Context (Auth, Theme, QueryClient, Global state), supply the required context wrapper using the `wrapper` option in renderHook() or render().
Lesson outcome: You should be able to test built-in hook behavior, custom hooks, state updates, asynchronous logic and hooks that depend on React Context.
6.1 What should be tested in a form?

Initial form state, required-field validation, incorrect input, valid input, submission behavior, error messages, loading state, success message, disabled controls, and duplicate submission prevention.
6.2 Understanding user-event

Testing Library user-event simulates real user actions (clicking, typing, selecting options, uploading files, keyboard interactions, clearing inputs) and is generally preferable to low-level event dispatch. (Testing Library)
npm install -D @testing-library/user-event
6.3 Building a simple registration form
6.4 Testing successful form submission
6.5 Testing validation errors
6.6 Testing keyboard interactions
Verify Tab, Shift + Tab, Enter, Space, Arrow keys, and Escape for accessibility and real-world usability.
6.7 Testing asynchronous form behavior
Verify all three states (Submitting loading state, Success confirmation, Failure error) and ensure accidental duplicate submissions are prevented while pending.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to test form validation, user interactions, keyboard behavior, submission states, error handling and success states.

sections.title: Mocking API Requests and External Dependencies

blocks.text: 7.1 What is mocking?
Mocking replaces a real dependency (backend API, auth provider, payment service, browser API) with a controlled substitute during testing.
7.2 Understanding different test doubles
Type | Meaning
Mock | Controlled replacement used to verify interactions or behavior
Stub | Supplies predefined responses
Fake | Lightweight working implementation of a dependency
Spy | Observes calls to an existing function or method
7.3 Using Vitest mock functions
7.4 Mocking a module
Vitest provides vi.mock() for module mocking and vi.spyOn() for spying on existing methods. (Vitest)
7.5 Understanding network-level mocking with MSW
Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts network requests at the network level so normal fetch logic remains intact.
7.6 Testing API failure scenarios
API response | Expected frontend behavior
200 OK | Display data
201 Created | Display successful creation
400 Bad Request | Show validation feedback
401 Unauthorized | Handle authentication failure
403 Forbidden | Show access-denied state
404 Not Found | Display missing-resource interface
500 Server Error | Show a recoverable error
Network failure | Display connection error
Also test empty arrays, missing fields, malformed responses, slow API responses, request cancellation, and retry behavior.
7.7 Playwright API mocking
Lesson outcome: Understand mocking, stubs, spies, fake dependencies, API testing, Vitest mocking and network-level mocking.
8.1 What is integration testing?
Integration testing evaluates the interaction between multiple application components, services or modules (e.g. search input + API service + results list).
8.2 Understanding an integrated feature
User -> Search Input -> Search Logic -> Course API -> Returned Data -> Course List -> Course Cards.
8.3 What should be tested?
Initial course loading, search query submission, category filtering, combined search and filtering, empty search results, API error handling, updating displayed results, and course navigation.
8.4 Example integration test
8.5 Integration testing vs unit testing

Unit testing tests individual logic with fewer dependencies and fast execution (e.g. search function). Integration testing tests combined functionality across dependencies with more realistic feature behavior (e.g. search input plus results).
8.6 Common integration failures

Test for incorrect data passed between components, unmapped API responses, stale search results, broken loading transitions, unpropagated errors, and race conditions where an older slower request overwrites newer results.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to test combined frontend features, data flow, API integration, search behavior, loading states and failure scenarios.
9.1 What is End-to-End testing?
End-to-End testing verifies whether an entire application workflow functions correctly from a user's perspective inside a real browser.
9.2 What is Playwright?

Playwright is a browser automation and testing framework supporting Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, assertions, network interception, screenshots, mobile emulation, test isolation, parallel execution, and trace-based debugging. (Playwright)
9.3 Installing Playwright
npm init playwright@latest
9.4 Understanding Playwright architecture
Test Specification -> Playwright Runner -> Browser (Chromium / Firefox / WebKit) -> React Application -> Assertions -> Test Results.
9.5 Your first Playwright test
tests/homepage.spec.ts
9.6 Understanding browser locators
Prefer locators based on accessible roles and labels rather than fragile CSS selectors.
9.7 Understanding browser interactions
Method | Purpose
click() | Click an element
fill() | Enter text into an input
check() | Check a checkbox
uncheck() | Uncheck a checkbox
selectOption() | Select an option
hover() | Hover over an element
press() | Perform keyboard actions
screenshot() | Capture a screenshot
goto() | Navigate to a URL
9.8 Understanding web-first assertions
Playwright automatically retries assertions and performs actionability checks before actions. (Playwright)
9.9 Building a complete student journey
9.10 Understanding Playwright configuration
playwright.config.ts
9.11 Understanding test reports and debugging
Playwright provides HTML reports, screenshots on failure, video recording, Trace Viewer, browser logs, network information, and DOM snapshots. (Playwright)
Lesson outcome: You should be able to install Playwright, write browser tests, use locators and assertions, automate user journeys and investigate failures.
10.1 What is cross-browser testing?
Cross-browser testing verifies that an application behaves consistently across supported browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) and browser environments.
10.2 Why does cross-browser testing matter?
Different browsers can render Flexbox/grid, unsupported CSS, dropdowns, form validation, animations, storage, and mobile menus differently.
10.3 Understanding browser engines
Browser | Main rendering engine
Google Chrome | Blink
Microsoft Edge | Blink
Mozilla Firefox | Gecko
Apple Safari | WebKit
10.4 Cross-browser testing with Playwright
10.5 Mobile and responsive testing
Device category | Example width
Small mobile | 360 px
Large mobile | 430 px
Tablet | 768 px
Laptop | 1366 px
Desktop | 1920 px
Test navigation menus, responsive cards, tables, forms, modals, sidebars, text wrapping, scroll behavior, and touch interactions.
10.6 Device emulation vs real-device testing
Browser emulation is useful for viewport/touch testing, while real devices reveal hardware-specific issues, OS differences, real keyboard behavior, and device performance limits.
Lesson outcome: Understand browser rendering differences, cross-browser automation and responsive testing using Chromium, Firefox, WebKit and device emulation.
11.1 What is web accessibility?

Web accessibility means designing and developing applications so people with disabilities (screen reader users, keyboard users, limited vision, hearing, motor, or cognitive disabilities) can perceive, understand, navigate, and interact with them.
11.2 Understanding WCAG
POUR principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.
11.3 Common accessibility problems
Problem | Possible consequence
Missing image alt text | Screen readers cannot communicate image meaning
Missing form labels | Users cannot identify inputs
Poor color contrast | Text becomes difficult to read
Keyboard-inaccessible menu | Keyboard users cannot navigate
Missing button names | Screen reader users cannot identify controls
Improper heading structure | Page structure becomes difficult to understand
Missing focus indicators | Keyboard position is unclear
11.4 Understanding semantic HTML
Prefer native elements such as <button>, <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <form>, <label>, and <a> over clickable <div> elements.
11.5 Testing keyboard accessibility
Verify Tab reachability, visible focus, keyboard button activation, menu keyboard controls, no focus traps, and modal focus management.
11.6 Understanding automated accessibility testing
npm install -D @axe-core/playwright
Combine automated checks with manual accessibility assessments and inclusive user testing. (Playwright)
11.7 Accessibility testing checklist
Verify alt text, form labels, color contrast, accessible button names, heading hierarchy, keyboard navigation, focus indicators, dialog focus management, zoom usability, and error announcements.
Lesson outcome: Understand WCAG principles, semantic HTML, keyboard accessibility, screen-reader considerations and automated audits using axe-core.
12.1 What is visual regression testing?
Visual regression testing compares the current appearance of an application against previously approved baseline screenshots.
12.2 Understanding screenshot comparison
Even when functional tests pass, CSS changes can break padding, typography, alignment, or responsive layouts. Visual regression tests detect these differences.
12.3 Visual testing with Playwright
12.4 What should you visually test?
UI element | What to verify
Navbar | Height, alignment and responsive menu
Course cards | Dimensions, text wrapping and spacing
Sidebar | Position and width
Dashboard | Layout consistency
Buttons | Size, placement and color
Forms | Input alignment and validation display
Mobile pages | Overflow and overlapping elements
Modals | Position and dimensions
12.5 Testing different viewport sizes
12.6 Understanding false positives

Font rendering differences, time-dependent content, animations, OS differences, and browser versions can cause false positives. Generate baselines in consistent environments, disable animations, and mask dynamic regions where appropriate.
12.7 Updating reference screenshots
npx playwright test --update-snapshots
Only update baselines after reviewing diffs and confirming intentional design changes.
Lesson outcome: You should be able to create screenshot baselines, compare visual changes, test responsive layouts and identify unintended UI regressions.
13.1 What is test coverage?
Test coverage measures which parts of your application code are executed during testing, though it does not by itself prove every behavior was correctly verified.
13.2 Types of code coverage
1. Statement coverage: Proportion of executable statements executed.
2. Branch coverage: Whether different decision paths (e.g. if/else) were executed.
3. Function coverage: How many functions were called.
4. Line coverage: How many executable lines were executed.
13.3 Understanding coverage metrics
Illustrative report: Statements 90%, Branches 75%, Functions 95%, Lines 88%.
13.4 Generating coverage reports in Vitest
npm install -D @vitest/coverage-v8
Run: npm run test:coverage (Vitest)
13.5 Understanding coverage thresholds
13.6 Why 100% coverage is not always enough
Executing a function achieves line coverage even if boundary conditions (zero, negative, invalid values) were never asserted. Focus on meaningful scenarios rather than percentages alone.
13.7 Understanding other quality metrics
Metric | What it measures
Test coverage | Code executed during testing
Test pass rate | Proportion of tests passing
Defect rate | Frequency of discovered defects
Regression rate | Frequency of previously fixed defects returning
Flaky test rate | Tests that produce inconsistent outcomes
Mean time to repair | Time required to diagnose and fix failures
Build success rate | Frequency of successful builds
Lesson outcome: Understand statement, branch, function and line coverage, generate reports using Vitest, establish coverage thresholds and evaluate quality beyond percentages.
14.1 What is Continuous Integration?
Continuous Integration (CI) automatically checks code changes through an automated build and testing workflow on push or pull request.
14.2 Why is CI important?
CI detects integration conflicts and regressions automatically when multiple developers merge changes.
14.3 Understanding a CI pipeline

Developer Changes Code -> Git Push -> GitHub Repository -> CI Workflow Starts -> (Linting, Tests, Type Check) -> Production Build -> E2E Testing -> All Checks Passed? -> Ready for Code Review / Release.
14.4 Understanding GitHub Actions
GitHub Actions automates installing dependencies, linting, unit tests, coverage reports, TypeScript checks, production builds, Playwright tests, and artifact preservation. (GitHub Docs)
14.5 Creating a CI workflow
.github/workflows/frontend-tests.yml

name: Frontend Quality Checks

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Run unit tests
        run: npm run test:run

      - name: Run coverage
        run: npm run test:coverage

      - name: Build application
        run: npm run build
14.6 Adding Playwright to CI

- name: Install Playwright browsers
        run: npx playwright install --with-deps

      - name: Run end-to-end tests
        run: npx playwright test
14.7 Understanding testing before deployment
Code Changes -> Pull Request -> Lint + Type Check -> Unit + Component Tests -> Integration Tests -> Production Build -> End-to-End Tests -> Code Review -> Merge -> Deployment.
14.8 Understanding failed CI checks
Inspect failed reports and screenshot diffs, fix unintended issues, and update approved baselines only when visual changes are deliberate.
Lesson outcome: Understand CI, GitHub Actions, automated quality gates, testing workflows, CI failure diagnosis and how to integrate testing before production deployment.

sections.title: Build an Automated Testing Suite for a React Application

blocks.text: Major practical project
Project objective

Build a complete automated testing system for a React application (such as the learning platform developed in previous modules) that detects functional defects, integration failures, browser compatibility issues, accessibility problems, and unintended visual changes.
1. Application under test
Feature | Application responsibility
Registration | Create a student account
Login | Authenticate a user
Homepage | Display platform information
Course catalogue | Show available courses
Course details | Display course descriptions
Search | Retrieve matching courses
Filtering | Filter by category or level
Student dashboard | Display progress
Lesson interface | Display lesson information
Progress tracking | Save completed lessons
Settings | Manage user preferences
2. Testing architecture

project/
├── src/
│   ├── components/
│   │   ├── CourseCard.tsx
│   │   ├── Navbar.tsx
│   │   └── LoginForm.tsx
│   ├── hooks/
│   │   └── useProgress.ts
│   ├── services/
│   │   └── courseService.ts
│   ├── utils/
│   │   └── calculateProgress.ts
│   └── test/
│       ├── setup.ts
│       └── server.ts
├── tests/
│   ├── unit/
│   ├── components/
│   ├── integration/
│   └── mocks/
├── e2e/
│   ├── authentication.spec.ts
│   ├── courses.spec.ts
│   ├── progress.spec.ts
│   └── navigation.spec.ts
├── playwright.config.ts
├── vitest.config.ts
└── package.json
3. Required testing scenarios
A. Unit testing: Course completion calculations, progress percentage, input validation, search filtering logic, sorting, data formatting, utilities, error-handling logic.
B. Component testing: Navbar, login form, registration form, course card, search input, course filters, progress indicator, modal dialogs, loading skeletons, error interfaces.
C. Hook testing: Custom progress hook, authentication state hook, search hook, theme preference hook, data-fetching hook.
D. API mocking: Successful API responses, empty responses, invalid responses, server errors, network failures, delayed responses, unauthorized requests.
E. Integration testing: Search input + course results, category filters + course lists, login form + auth service, progress updates + course interface, API responses + error messages.
F. End-to-End testing:
Journey 1 — Student registration: Open Registration -> Enter Student Details -> Submit Form -> Validate Input -> Account Created -> Confirmation Displayed.
Journey 2 — Student learning: Open Website -> Login -> Open Course Catalogue -> Select Course -> Open Lesson -> Complete Lesson -> Verify Progress Updated.
Journey 3 — Search and filtering: Open Courses -> Enter Search Query -> Select Category -> Display Matching Courses -> Open Selected Course.
G. Accessibility testing: Keyboard navigation, accessible names, form labels, alt text, color contrast, heading hierarchy, dialog focus behavior, automated axe-core reports.
H. Visual regression testing: Approved screenshots of Homepage (desktop/mobile), Course catalogue (desktop/mobile), Course details, Student dashboard, Login and registration pages.
I. Cross-browser testing: Run critical user journeys in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, plus mobile and tablet viewports.
4. Project implementation checklist
1. Configure Vitest and React Testing Library — Install testing dependencies and configure the DOM environment.
2. Create unit tests — Test calculations, utilities, validations and boundary conditions.
3. Create component tests — Verify rendering, accessible elements and component behavior.
4. Test custom hooks — Verify state changes, asynchronous behavior and context dependencies.
5. Test forms and user interactions — Cover validation, submission, loading and error states.
6. Configure API mocking — Use controlled responses for successful and failed requests.
7. Create integration tests — Test search, filtering, API integration and application features.
8. Configure Playwright — Set up browser automation, test configuration and reports.
9. Automate user journeys — Test registration, login, course navigation and progress tracking.
10. Configure cross-browser testing — Run the suite in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
11. Implement accessibility audits — Run automated accessibility scans and keyboard checks.
12. Implement visual regression tests — Establish screenshot baselines for desktop and mobile.
13. Generate coverage reports — Measure statements, functions, branches and lines.
14. Configure GitHub Actions — Automate tests, coverage checks and production builds.
5. Final project evaluation
Evaluation area | Expected result
Unit testing | Important application logic covered
Component testing | UI components behave correctly
Hook testing | Reusable stateful logic verified
Form testing | Valid and invalid submissions tested
API mocking | Success and failure scenarios covered
Integration | Combined features work correctly
E2E testing | Critical user journeys pass
Cross-browser | Supported browser projects pass
Accessibility | Automated audits and manual checks
Visual testing | Unintended visual changes detected
Coverage | Meaningful reports and thresholds
CI | Automated checks execute on code changes
Final deliverable: A reusable automated frontend testing suite that can be executed locally and through a CI pipeline, with test reports and documented testing decisions.

sections.title: Advanced Testing Concepts, Resources & Completion Standard

blocks.text: Additional advanced concepts to master
Concept | Why it matters
Property-Based Testing | Tests many generated inputs against defined properties
Mutation Testing | Checks whether tests detect deliberately introduced defects
Contract Testing | Verifies expectations between frontend and backend
Performance Testing | Measures application responsiveness and resource usage
Load Testing | Evaluates application behavior under traffic
Flaky Test Management | Identifies inconsistent automated tests
Test Data Management | Creates predictable and isolated test data
Visual Test Management | Manages screenshot baselines and approvals
Test-Driven Development | Develops functionality through a test-first workflow
Exploratory Testing | Finds unexpected defects through human investigation
Recommended learning resources
[Playwright documentation](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro) — E2E, browser automation, assertions and visual testing.
[Vitest documentation](https://vitest.dev/guide/) — unit testing, mocking, assertions and coverage.
[React Testing Library documentation](https://testing-library.com/docs/react-testing-library/intro/) — component testing and user-centered interactions.
[Playwright accessibility guide](https://playwright.dev/docs/accessibility-testing) — automated accessibility auditing with axe and Playwright.
[Visual regression testing](https://playwright.dev/docs/test-snapshots)
[Network and API mocking](https://playwright.dev/docs/network)
[Vitest coverage](https://vitest.dev/guide/coverage.html)
[Next.js testing guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/testing)
[GitHub Actions and Node.js testing](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/build-and-test-code/nodejs)

Important connection with Module 11: Apply these testing techniques to Next.js App Router applications as well. One current limitation to understand is that Vitest does not yet support testing asynchronous Server Components directly; Next.js recommends End-to-End testing for those components. Synchronous Server Components and Client Components can still be unit tested. (Next.js)
What students should be able to build after this module
Automated test suites: Unit, component and integration tests.
Browser automation: Automated user journeys and regression checks.
Visual quality assurance: Screenshot comparisons and responsive UI verification.
CI testing pipelines: Automated quality gates before deployment.

Module completion standard: Students should not merely know how to write test cases. They should be able to decide what needs testing, select the right testing strategy, simulate realistic user behavior, reproduce failure scenarios, measure meaningful coverage and prevent unverified code from reaching production.
